collection: NERDC JSS 1 Physical and Health Education recreation and athletics
note: Original classroom practice. Athletics uses video and tabletop observation rather than live jumps. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the take-off phase from flight in a long jump.
questions.prompt: A pupil pauses a video of a long jump just after the jumper’s take-off foot has left the ground. Which event marks the transition shown?
questions.answer: The jumper finishes pushing against the ground and begins moving through the air.
questions.explanation: Take-off ends when ground contact ends. Flight continues until the jumper touches down.
options: The jumper begins the approach run.
The jumper finishes pushing against the ground and begins moving through the air.
The jumper’s feet first contact the landing area.
The jumper stands and leaves the landing area.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Use a reference line and the nearest landing mark to measure a classroom trial.
questions.prompt: In a supervised tabletop officiating simulation, a drawn line represents take-off and a paper strip represents the sand. The teacher marks a heel print farther from the line and a hand print closer to it. The classroom rule uses the closest landing mark. Use a ruler to demonstrate the shortest measurement from the line to the appropriate mark. Report the distance with its unit.
questions.answer: Measure perpendicular from the line to the nearer hand mark, and report the ruler reading in the units shown. The rule uses the nearest mark left in the landing area.
questions.explanation: The classroom simulation isolates the measurement decision without requiring pupils to jump.

markingGuide.description: Uses the take-off line as the reference.
Reads and reports the measured distance with its unit.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish landing and recovery when observing a high jump.
questions.prompt: A teacher pauses a demonstration video twice. At frame A the jumper first contacts the landing mat. At frame B the jumper has settled and is getting up to leave. Name the phase shown by each frame and describe the difference.
questions.answer: Frame A shows landing, when the jumper first contacts the mat. Frame B shows recovery, when the jumper regains control after landing and prepares to leave.
questions.explanation: Landing begins at contact. Recovery takes place after that contact as the jumper comes to rest or regains control.

markingGuide.description: Explains the distinction using contact and regaining control.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish time available for leisure from a recreational activity during it.
questions.prompt: During a free period after school duties, pupils choose to play a clapping game for enjoyment. Identify the leisure time and the recreation in this example.
questions.answer: The free period is the leisure time. Playing the clapping game for enjoyment is the recreation.
questions.explanation: Leisure can describe time free from duties. Recreation describes an activity chosen for enjoyment or refreshment during free time.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the free period as leisure time.
Identifies the chosen clapping game as recreation.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an inclusive recreational activity can support social connection.
questions.prompt: A lunchtime movement game lets pupils choose a seated or standing role, and rotates who leads each round. Explain how these two features could help pupils join in and get to know one another.
questions.answer: Choice of role makes participation possible for more pupils. Rotating leaders gives different pupils opportunities to guide the group and gives others a reason to pay attention to each of them.
questions.explanation: Participation choices lower barriers and shared responsibility can encourage interaction.

markingGuide.description: Explains how rotating leadership creates opportunities for interaction.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Perform a simple group recreation activity using a shared pulse and turn-taking.
questions.prompt: In groups of three under teacher supervision, play a turn-taking rhythm game. Keep a gentle shared pulse. Each pupil gives one short clap or tap pattern for the others to echo before the next leader begins. Agree on a cue for changing leaders. A seated version is acceptable.
questions.answer: One pupil gives a short two-tap pattern and the others echo it on the shared pulse. The agreed cue passes leadership to the next pupil until each has led.
questions.explanation: The shared pulse helps the group respond together, and rotating turns makes participation visible.

markingGuide.description: Gives a short pattern during the assigned turn.
Uses or responds to the agreed turn-changing cue.
